damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 31 – Aberforth confrontation at the Hog's Head
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Aberforth's grievance as deeply personal and specific: Albus neglected Ariana while consumed by his friendship with Grindelwald and plans for wizard domination. Aberforth recounts in detail how Albus was 'always up in his bedroom reading his books and counting his prizes,' how Grindelwald used the Cruciatus Curse on Aberforth, how Albus failed to defend him, and how Ariana died in the ensuing fight. Harry internally resolves his doubts by deciding to trust the Dumbledore he knew, having already made peace with Dumbledore's flawed past during Dobby's burial. Harry's resolution is earned through sustained internal wrestling across many chapters.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Aberforth's accusation is reduced to a single vague line: 'My brother sacrificed many things in his journey to find power, including her. She was devoted to him — he gave her everything, but time.' No detail about Grindelwald's abuse, the duel, or the circumstances of Ariana's death is given. Harry's counter-resolution — 'I only care about the Dumbledore I knew. I trusted him' / 'I need to. Because if I don't, I don't know who I am anymore' — arrives almost immediately and without the weight of the book's prolonged crisis of faith. The emotional arc of Harry reconciling with Dumbledore's flawed legacy is collapsed into a brief exchange.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book spends dozens of pages having Harry genuinely doubt Dumbledore — his wisdom, his care, his honesty — before arriving at a hard-won trust. The film skips the substance of Aberforth's full testimony (no Grindelwald detail, no Cruciatus, no three-way duel, no ambiguity about who killed Ariana) and rushes Harry's reconciliation. This collapses a major arc beat: the audience never fully understands why Harry had reason to doubt, so his decision to trust feels like stubbornness rather than hard-won faith. Dumbledore's moral complexity is also significantly flattened.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 37 – Headmaster's office: Dumbledore instructs Snape to kill him
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Dumbledore's request as morally and psychologically layered. He acknowledges Snape's soul may be harmed, frames it as a favour to spare himself pain and to protect Draco, and engages Snape on whether it will harm his soul. The conversation also covers Dumbledore's broader plan for the Elder Wand — that he intended to die undefeated so the wand's power would be broken. Dumbledore's tone is measured, almost philosophical, and he shows genuine concern for Snape's moral integrity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Dumbledore thunders: 'Too much! Nothing I could ask is too much. You know what is at stake! You more than anyone!' This outburst replaces the book's quiet, collaborative moral reasoning. The nuanced discussion about Snape's soul, Draco's soul, and Dumbledore's personal wish to avoid a painful death is absent. Dumbledore sounds coercive and self-righteous rather than wise and self-aware.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Dumbledore in this scene is characterised by calm acceptance of death and genuine solicitude for Snape's soul. The film replaces this with an uncharacteristic outburst that makes Dumbledore sound demanding and domineering. This undermines the portrait of a man who has accepted mortality with serenity and who treats Snape as a moral agent rather than an instrument.

damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book's King's Cross scene is extensive. Dumbledore confesses his entire history with Grindelwald and the Hallows at length, including his resentment of his family, his ambition, his cowardice in delaying the confrontation with Grindelwald for fear of learning he killed Ariana, his self-loathing, his recognition that he was unfit for power, his explanation of why he refused the Ministry of Magic, and his full account of obtaining the Elder Wand. He explicitly asks Harry for forgiveness and describes himself as 'a fool' and 'less than a good man.' The scene also resolves the Snitch, the Resurrection Stone, the Cloak's lineage, Lily's sacrifice mechanics, and Voldemort's use of Harry's blood. Harry defends Dumbledore from Dumbledore's own self-criticism.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's King's Cross retains key plot mechanics (Horcrux explanation, Harry's choice to return, 'pity the living') but strips almost all of Dumbledore's confession and self-reckoning. There is no admission of cowardice about Grindelwald, no account of why he refused the Ministry, no extended discussion of the Hallows obsession, no explanation of the Resurrection Stone's personal meaning (only a brief mention of Ariana), and no Harry defending Dumbledore from himself. The scene's emotional substance — Dumbledore weeping, looking 'less than an old man,' asking forgiveness — is largely absent. Instead the film adds invented wordplay ('Help will always be given… to those who most deserve it') and comic asides about miracles and luck.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the saga's primary scene of Dumbledore's moral reckoning and self-revelation. The book uses it to complete Harry's understanding of Dumbledore as a flawed, brilliant, deeply human figure who grew from his failures. The film replaces much of this with plot logistics and tonal lightness, so the audience never receives the full portrait: Dumbledore as a man humbled by his own past, who earned wisdom through shame. The structural consequence is that Dumbledore's arc — from youthful arrogance to redemptive wisdom to humble self-knowledge — is only partially conveyed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 – Forest of Dean: Hermione reveals Grindelwald connection
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Harry's crisis of faith in Dumbledore as a sustained, multi-chapter internal experience. Harry reads the Skeeter biography himself, is consumed by rage and grief, wrestles with whether Dumbledore ever truly cared for him, and arrives at anguished questions: 'Had Dumbledore actually cared about Harry at all? Or had Harry been nothing more than a tool?' Harry bellows his grievance: 'Look what he asked from me… Risk your life, Harry! And again! And again! And don't expect me to explain everything, just trust me blindly… Never the whole truth! Never!' Hermione's counter-argument is also developed at length.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Hermione narrates the Grindelwald backstory to Harry efficiently and Harry's reaction is relatively contained: he states 'We're young, Hermione. And here we are, risking our lives to fight against the very thing Dumbledore supported,' then tosses the book away and asks for his wand. The scene is followed immediately by the broken wand revelation, which redirects emotional focus. Harry's multi-chapter internal crisis — the rage, the sense of betrayal, the specific accusation that Dumbledore used him as a tool — is not dramatised in depth.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's portrait of Harry's disillusionment with Dumbledore is one of the character's most important emotional developments in the saga. It shows Harry as capable of genuine anger toward his mentor and deepens his eventual decision to trust Dumbledore anyway. The film conveys the fact of the revelation but not its emotional weight, so Harry's later declaration of trust (at Aberforth's) carries less resonance.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 – Will reading at the Burrow (Scrimgeour scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book's will-reading scene includes a full confrontation between Harry and Scrimgeour, in which Harry challenges the Ministry's cowardice, references Voldemort chasing him, and Scrimgeour physically grabs Harry before catching himself. The scene establishes Harry as willing to confront authority on Dumbledore's behalf and demonstrates Scrimgeour's desperation. Dumbledore's specific wording in the will — 'in the hope that he will remember me when he uses it' (Deluminator) — carries emotional resonance about Dumbledore's foresight.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The will-reading is present and reasonably faithful in structure. Scrimgeour delivers the bequests, Ron demonstrates the Deluminator, Hermione receives Beedle. However, the charged confrontation between Harry and Scrimgeour — Harry's accusations about Ministry cowardice, Scrimgeour grabbing Harry's arm, the physical tension — is replaced by Harry's cooler line 'it's a little hard to tell the difference these days.' The scene ends quietly with Scrimgeour leaving, looking haunted.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene to show Harry as fiercely loyal to Dumbledore's legacy and willing to confront the Minister of Magic directly on those grounds. The film softens this into mild wit. While not a major loss, Harry's passionate defence of Dumbledore's honour — one of the character's defining traits — is muted.

damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book's Pensieve sequence includes the hilltop scene (Dumbledore showing contempt: 'You disgust me… You do not care, then, about the deaths of her husband and child?'), the post-death office scene, the Yule Ball corridor (Dumbledore: 'You are a braver man by far than Igor Karkaroff. You know, I sometimes think we Sort too soon…'), the grounds walk where Dumbledore refuses to share the full plan with Snape and Snape accuses him of not trusting him, and the crucial office scene where Snape casts the Patronus. Dumbledore's 'After all this time?' / Snape's 'Always' exchange is the emotional climax. The sequence also contains Dumbledore instructing Snape via portrait.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes the hilltop scene (compressed, with 'You would sacrifice the life of an innocent child over a schoolboy crush?' replacing the book's more damning 'You do not care, then, about the deaths of her husband and child?'), the post-death office scene, and a brief Hogwarts grounds walk compressed into a single outdoor scene. The Yule Ball corridor scene — with Dumbledore's acknowledgment of Snape's bravery — is absent from the corpus. The portrait instruction scene (Dumbledore's portrait directing Snape to plant the sword) is absent. The emotional arc is present but the Yule Ball scene's tribute to Snape's courage (delivered by Dumbledore himself) is lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Yule Ball corridor scene is the only moment in the saga where Dumbledore explicitly acknowledges Snape's bravery to his face and reflects on the Sorting. Its absence slightly diminishes Dumbledore's characterisation as someone who sees deeply into people and honours sacrifice privately. The portrait instruction scene is also absent, removing evidence of Dumbledore's posthumous agency in protecting Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 40 – Viaduct: Harry breaks the Elder Wand
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has Harry return the Elder Wand to Dumbledore's tomb rather than destroying it, after a conversation with Dumbledore's portrait. Harry explains his reasoning to the portrait ('If I die a natural death like Ignotus, its power will be broken'). Dumbledore nods with satisfaction. The decision honours Dumbledore's wish that the wand's power die with its last undefeated master, and Harry acts in explicit dialogue with Dumbledore's legacy.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Harry snaps the Elder Wand and throws it off a viaduct. There is no consultation with Dumbledore's portrait, no Dumbledore presence in the resolution at all. The decision is Harry's alone, arrived at silently.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's ending explicitly shows Harry acting in partnership with Dumbledore's legacy — his final decision about the most powerful wand in existence is made in conversation with his mentor's portrait. The film removes Dumbledore entirely from this climactic choice and also changes the decision itself (destruction vs. return to tomb). This severs the relational thread of Harry and Dumbledore's partnership at the saga's conclusion and removes Dumbledore's posthumous agency from the resolution.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 – Wedding: Doge and Muriel conversation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book's wedding scene includes Harry's extended conversation with Doge and Muriel, in which specific allegations about Ariana (Squib vs. ill health), Kendra's cruelty, the coffin-side brawl, and Bathilda's role are raised. Harry is shaken and conflicted. The scene establishes the specific charges Harry will later have to reckon with.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Doge-Muriel scene is present but significantly compressed. Muriel mentions Bathilda Bagshot and Godric's Hollow, and Dumbledore's father killing three Muggles, but the specific allegations about Ariana being a Squib, Kendra imprisoning her, and the coffin-side brawl are absent. Muriel's line 'did he ever mention hers?' (Ariana) is the only hint at the family secret.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The specific allegations from the book — Ariana as a Squib, Kendra's cruel imprisonment, the funeral brawl — are what seed Harry's crisis of faith in Dumbledore throughout the middle of the story. The film's compressed version reduces the audience's sense of why Harry's doubts are serious and specific rather than vague unease.

main_damage_causes: Collapse of Harry's sustained crisis of faith in Dumbledore: the book's multi-chapter arc of doubt, rage, and hard-won reconciliation is compressed into brief exchanges, removing the emotional weight from Harry's eventual decision to trust

Truncation of the King's Cross scene's confessional depth: Dumbledore's full self-reckoning — cowardice about Grindelwald, refusal of Ministry power, self-loathing, extended apology — is largely replaced by plot logistics and tonal lightness, preventing the audience from receiving Dumbledore's complete moral portrait

Removal of Dumbledore's posthumous agency and relational presence at the saga's end: the portrait consultation over the Elder Wand and other instances of Dumbledore acting through legacy and foresight are cut, so the film's Dumbledore is a figure remembered rather than one whose plans and relationships continue to shape events
